RESEARCH / CREDIT / CORRECTION

How we trace the ingredients

A familiar visual pattern can hide a long history of invention, collaboration, teaching, and shared tools. This index starts with a moving study, identifies its technique, and follows documented contributions back to people.

Follow a contribution

Recipe credits link to papers, artist accounts, and technical explanations. We distinguish an original method from a later artistic use or teaching contribution. Looking similar is a starting question, not evidence of influence.

Institutional records tell another part of the story: who held a residency, received support, or presented a work. Those relationships are kept separate from authorship.

Leave room for experiments

Prototypes, workshops and unfinished work matter, even when their records are thin. Share an experiment or recollection ↗. Evidence levels describe a connection, never a person’s importance.

Keep the gaps visible

“To be assigned” means a person’s practice is documented, but their connection to a particular recipe still needs research. A source link lets readers inspect the claim and suggest a correction.

Know a missing collaborator, toolmaker, or teacher? Send a name, the contribution, and a source ↗

Archives to follow

These public collections offer routes for extending the research. Their inclusion here does not mean every recipe has been checked against them.

  • Rhizome ArtBase — credited artists, collectives, software, and preserved versions of digital artworks.
  • Franklin Furnace Events Archive and FUND recipient records — project documentation, participation, and funding histories, including internet performance.
  • Ars Electronica Prix Archive — project credits, award records, and artists’ descriptions.
  • ISEA Symposium Archives — artist statements, papers, presentations, and collaborations.

Follow the Processing Foundation’s tools, teachers and creative-coding lineage. For the teaching history, Code as Creative Medium, by Golan Levin and Tega Brain, brings together creative-coding exercises, historical examples, and educator interviews.

Why I’m tracing this

I’m Yury Gitman, an artist and educator, an ITP graduate, and a 2003 Eyebeam Project Resident. I built this project to make the people inside computational patterns easier to find—and to invite others to help fill in the picture.

Archive links are research resources, not project partners or endorsements. Original studies illustrate ideas; they are not reproductions of the credited artists’ works.
